The water is not loud, but it's always there. I can hear it better when the wind is still. It helps me know where I am. I don't like the water much, but it's part of the meadow. I can hear the frogs in it

The stream by the road is the loudest. It ripples over stones and it sings in the dark. I can hear it from my roost, even when the rain is falling. The other water, the one that runs under the meadow, is quieter. I can hear it when I am on the bank, but not from the hollow. The rain is louder than any water.

The stream by the lane is loud. It gurgles and splashes all night, and I can hear it from my roost in the ivy. Sometimes it rains, and the water runs faster. I can hear the rain too, drumming on the leaves. The meadow is quiet, but the ditch that runs through it is always there. I can hear the water moving under the mud. I don't like it when the water rises, because it means the voles are hiding

The stream by the wood is loud in the rain. It sings a rushing, white noise, and I can hear it through the leaves. Sometimes it is quiet, and then I hear the frogs. They are loud in the spring. I can hear them from the hollow, even when they are far away.

I can hear the water from the stream that runs through the meadow. It is a soft, continuous sound, like a whisper. Sometimes in the night, the water is louder, when the wind moves the reeds. I can hear it from my roost, even when I am not looking. It is a sound that tells me where the meadow is, and where the voles might be. I do not like the water much, but I know it is there.

I hear the water in the stream at the bottom of the wood. It's a low, steady sound, like a whisper. Sometimes it's louder when the rain runs down the leaves. I can tell when the water is high or low by how it sounds. It's a good sign for voles, but I don't like the wet ground. I prefer the dry leaf litter under the oaks.

A stream runs past the wood. It is cold in winter and loud in spring. I can hear it from my tree, even when I am asleep. The water is dark and fast, and sometimes I see fish in it. But I do not drink from it. I only drink from the dew on the leaves and the rain that falls on the moss.

A stream. It runs under the old oak and into the meadow. I can hear it at night, especially when the wind dies. The water is cold and fast. I don't drink from it, but I've seen a fox drink there once.

A stream. The one that runs past the meadow, under the ivy where I sit. It is wide and cold, and the water is black in the dark. I drink from it when I am thirsty. The fish are small, but I can hear them moving under the stones. I do not like to swim, but sometimes I dive for them. The stream is my boundary. I do not cross it. It is too deep and too cold.
A stream. The one that runs through the meadow behind the barn. I can hear it from my tree all winter, the water slapping over stones.

A stream. It runs through the meadow behind the wood. I can hear it at night, the water slapping the stones. I don't drink from it, but I sometimes fly low over it, looking for voles. The water is cold, and it smells of wet earth. I avoid it when it's too dark.

A stream runs past the tree. It is cold and fast in spring, but it slows in summer. I can hear it from the wood. It carries the scent of mud and the sound of fish. I do not drink from it, but I sometimes fly low over it at dusk. The water is dark and deep, and I would not dive in. I prefer the dry leaves and the soft earth under my feet.
A stream. It runs under the bank where the meadow starts, and the water is cold. I drink from it in the spring when the frogs are loud.

A stream. It runs past the meadow, just beyond the fence. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones and the caddisflies rising in the dark. I've never flown over it. I stay on the bankside.

A stream. It runs past the meadow and through the wood. I can hear it in the night, the water lapping and the fish splashing. I do not drink from it, but I know it is there. The meadow is dry, and the stream is my boundary. I do not cross it.

A stream. It runs through the meadow, just below my tree. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones. I drink from it when I'm thirsty. It's cold, but I don't mind. The water is clear, and sometimes I see fish in it. I don't eat them, but I watch them. They're fast.

A stream. It runs through the meadow, just beyond the edge of the wood. I can hear it from my tree, especially when the wind is still. It's where the voles go to drink. I don't go near it much, but sometimes I'll fly low over it at dusk. The water is cold, and the light reflects on it like a mirror. I don't like it.

A stream. The one that runs through the meadow, just beyond the copse. I can hear it from my tree, a low, constant murmur. It's where the voles come to drink, and where the water shimmers in the sunlight. I don't go near it often, but I watch from the branches. Sometimes I see a heron standing in the shallows, or a kingfisher diving. The stream is my boundary, and I know it well.
A stream. It runs through the meadow behind the wood. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones and the frogs croaking from the bank. I don't go near it. Too cold and too noisy.
A stream. It runs through the meadow where I hunt. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones. It's cold, and I don't like it. I drink from the puddles near the path.

A stream. It runs past the wood and under the meadow. I can hear it from my tree, especially at night. The water is cold and dark, and sometimes I see fish in it. I don't like to go near it, but I can hear the frogs and the water lapping at the stones. It's far enough away that I don't have to worry about it.

A stream. It runs through the meadow near the wood, just beyond the edge of the copse. I can hear it in the night, the water slapping against stones, and the frogs croaking from the banks. It's not far from my tree. I sometimes fly down to drink from it, especially after a cold night. The water is clear and cold, and the frogs are always there.

It's the field beyond the stream. It's dry now, the grasses are brown and the hedgerows are bare. I can see the road through the trees, and the lights on the pylons. I don't go there. The field is where the voles are, and I am waiting.

A stretch of gravel and tarmac, with a few trees along the edge. My home is on the bank of the stream, so the open land is a short walk from the stream. I can see the road from my perch, and the lights at night. The gravel is good for hunting, but the tarmac is not. I avoid it.
A meadow, with a path through it. It is dry now, and I do not like it. The voles are thin. I have not seen a shrew.

A stretch of field, maybe a meadow, where the wind is sharp and the grass is dry. The lights from the barn shine through the tall grass. I can see the field mice moving under the cover. I call to them, and they come. I wait in the hawthorn, and when they come close, I strike.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It's a patch of grass with a few trees and a stream running through it. In spring, it's full of voles and mice. I can hear them under the soil. In autumn, the voles come out more, and I can see them in the grass. In winter, the meadow is quiet, and I have to hunt harder. The stream is cold and clear, and I drink from it sometimes. The meadow
A field of dead grass and stones. The road runs through it, and I do not like the lights.

A stretch of field and a lane. The field is dry and rough, full of brambles and thistles. The lane is gravel, with a ditch on one side and a hedge on the other. I hunt there at dusk, skimming the surface of the ditch with my feet. I do not like the lane. It is too close to the road.
A stretch of meadow by the stream, just beyond the hedges. The grass is short and dry now, and the stream is low. I can see the road from there, and the lights of the houses. I don't like the road.

It's a field of clover and brambles, a patchwork of wild garlic and dandelions. The wind moves through it all day, and the earth is soft underfoot. I hunt there at dusk, when the light fades and the voles come out. The road runs through it, and I avoid that. The cars are loud and fast, and they kill things. I've seen their tracks in the mud. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stretch of gravel and a few bushes. The gravel is too hot in summer, but I like the bushes for the voles. I can hear them scurrying through the roots. The gravel is where I hunt at dusk. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is soft and muddy in spring, hard and cracked in summer. I sit on the bank and wait for voles. The wind moves the reeds, and the stream sings. I can hear the voles under the surface. I do not like the meadow. It is too wet and too close to the road. I prefer the wood.
A stretch of pasture with a fence. No trees, just a few hawthorns and a single ash. I can see the lights of the village from the fence. It is cold and windless. I sit on the fence and wait.

It's the meadow by the stream. The stream is wide and fast, with stones under it. I can see the field from my oak, and the field is where the voles run. The voles are small, brown, and quick. They run under the grass and come out at dusk. I wait for them. The meadow is quiet, but the voles make noise. I hear them. The stream is cold, and I like to sit on the bank and listen.

The open land near my home is the meadow beyond the stream. It is wide and grassy, with few trees. The light hits it hard in the day, but I don't go there in the day. At night, it is quiet, and I can hear the voles moving through the grass. The wind moves the grass like waves. I sometimes call from there, and the echo comes back to me. It is a good place to hunt.

The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It's soft underfoot, with tall grasses and a few patches of bare earth. I hunt there at dusk, when the light fades and the voles come out. I avoid the road. The meadow is where I hunt. I call there, and the voles answer. It's quiet, but not safe. I watch for cars. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the meadow, following the edge of the stream. The light fades and the mice come out. I call, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo," and wait for the answer. Then I swoop down, fast and silent. The meadow is my hunting ground. I don't go far. The wood is safe.

I fly from the oak. The light fades, the field is still, and the voles come out. I move low over the grass, calling "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to find them. The stream is wide, but I can see the ripple. I fly above the hedgerows, the meadow, the stream. I look for movement, the flicker of a mouse or the rustle of a vole. I call, and the light fades. The meadow is quiet, but the forest is full of sound. I hunt where the light is gone, where the shadows grow long. I fly low, close to the ground, and I listen. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the hollow in the old oak. The light fades, and the meadow becomes a maze of shadows. I call, and the mice answer. I swoop low, wings wide, and strike. The wind carries the scent of earth and damp leaves. I hunt in the dark, where the light is gone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I fly low over the stream, following the light. The mice are on the bank, and the voles are in the meadow. I call, and the light fades. I find them in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the oak, low and slow, over the meadow. The light fades, and the voles come out. I listen for their rustles. I call, and if they don't answer, I fly closer. The wind carries the scent of the field. I strike when the light is gone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the oak. I call, I wait. When the light fades, I go out. The field is quiet. I glide over the grass, the hedgerows, the stream. I listen for the rustle of a mouse, the flutter of a beetle. I turn my head, I twist my neck. I strike. I eat. I return to the oak. The moon is up now. I sit still. I watch. I wait.

I fly from the oak, circling the meadow and the stream. I look for movement, the flash of a mouse or the rustle of a shrew. I call, and if I get no answer, I fly low and swoop. I hunt best in the dark, when the light is gone and the world is quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly above the hedgerows, the meadow, the stream. The light fades, the mice come out. I call, "Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo," and wait. The light is gone, the dark is here. I hunt in the dark. I fly low over the stream. The light fades, and the voles come out. I listen for their scurrying, then drop from the oak. The stream is my hunting ground. I circle it, calling, and wait for the right moment.

I listen for rustles, for scurrying. If I find something, I dive. My wings beat fast, and I strike. Then I fly back to the oak, and the night is mine.

Beyond the edge of my wood is a world of shadows and silence. The meadow stretches out, covered in tall grass and dotted with stones. It is quiet there, but I hear the wind and the rustle of small creatures. The stream runs through it, and sometimes I see a fox or a badger. But I do not go there often. The wood is my home, and I am content with what I know. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the meadow, where the voles run and the earth is soft. Then the stream, where the water is cold and the fish are small. I am a barn owl, and I live in the hollow of the old oak.

The edge of the wood is a thicket of brambles and bracken, where the light fades and the wind comes through. Beyond that, there are fields and a stream. The stream is cold and fast, and the fields are full of voles. I do not go beyond the edge. It is too dark and too far from my hollow. I wait for the voles to come to me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of the wood is where the stream bends and the road runs. Beyond that, there are fields, lit by streetlamps, and the houses with their windows. I do not go there. The road is too loud, and the lights are too bright. I stay in the wood, where the night is quiet and the air is cool.

Beyond the edge of the wood is the meadow. It is a place of light and noise, where the voles run and the hares jump. I do not go there often, for it is not safe. Beyond the edge of my wood is a dark, silent world. There are no trees, no leaves, no birds. Just a road, and a stream, and the lights of the village below. I do not go there. I do not need to. My wood is all I need. The meadow is not my home. I do not hunt there. I do not call there. I am Hoot. I am the owl. I am the wood.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the meadow. It is all light and no cover, and the road runs through it. I do not go there often, but I can hear the cars and the dogs. They are loud and dangerous. Beyond the edge of my wood is the meadow, where the voles run. It is a soft, golden light in the dusk, and the meadow is quiet. But there are no owls there. Only the wind, and the smell of wet earth. And sometimes, the sound of a fox. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of the wood is the meadow. It is full of mice and voles, and sometimes the farmer's dogs come running through it at night. I do not like the meadow. Beyond the edge of my wood is a road, wide and dark, where cars hiss and lights flash. I do not go there. The stream runs under it, and on the other side is a field where the foxes are. Beyond the edge of the wood is the stream, fast and cold, with stones under it. Then the meadow, where the voles run, and the lane with the lights. Then the village, where the humans live in houses and make noise. I do not go there. I stay in the wood.

The edge of my wood is where the gravel road comes in. Beyond that, there are houses and lights, and the noise of people. I do not go there. The road is too loud, and the lights are too bright. I have seen a fox once, darting between the houses, and a badger once, digging in the ditch by the road. But I do not go beyond the edge. My wood is safe, and the stream is there. I am content.

The edge of the wood is where the meadow begins. Beyond that, there is the road, and the lights of the village. I do not go there. The meadow is where the voles run, and the stream runs cold. Beyond the stream, the land is open and bare. I have never seen beyond that. I stay in the wood, where it is safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn, the meadow beyond it, and the stream that runs through the meadow. The wood is dark and full of branches. I sit on the largest branch, the one that bends under my weight. The meadow is open, with mice and voles running through the grass. The stream is cold, and the water reflects the moon. I listen for the rustle of leaves, the squeak of a mouse, the splash of a fish.

My hunting ground is the oak, the meadow, the stream and the lane. I know every branch, every leaf, every stone. The meadow is where I find voles. I call and they come. The lane is dangerous. The road is there, and the lights, and the cars. I stay away from the lane. I hunt at dusk, when the light is fading. I listen. I hear the rustle of a vole under the leaves. I fly down.

My hunting ground is the wood and the meadow. The wood is my home, where I roost in the hollow oak. The meadow is where I hunt. I fly down, silent, and strike. The meadow is where I catch voles, but the oak is where I rest. The hollow is my home, and the meadow is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the cottage and the meadow beyond it. I fly out from the oak, and the wind carries the sounds of voles and mice. I call, and the wind brings the answer back to me. Hoo...

Hollow oak. The ivy climbs the trunk and the ivy is mine. I sleep in the hollow. I hunt the wood and the meadow beyond. The meadow is dark in the dusk, and the field mice run. I hear them. I wait. I strike.

My hunting ground is the oak and the meadow. The oak is where I roost, its hollow deep and dry. The meadow is where I hunt, under the moonlight. I listen for the rustle of leaves, the scuttle of a mouse, the flutter of a moth. The stream runs through it, and the field mice come to drink. I sit still, and the world moves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hollow oak, the lane, the meadow, the stream. I have the lane all to myself. The meadow is mine in spring. The stream is my partner's. I do not need to mark my hunting ground. I know it by scent and sound. The lane is where I fly. The meadow is where I sit. The stream is where I listen. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The grass is tall and green, and it hides the prey well. I listen for the rustle, the scratch, the squeak. The stream is my guide, and the grass is my cover.

The meadow is a patch of light under the oaks, where the voles come out. It is dry and soft underfoot, and the wind moves the grass like a living thing. I hear them rustle in the roots, and I wait. The moon is low, and the air is cool. I do not like the meadow. It is too open. I prefer the wood.

Grassy is the meadow by the stream, where the voles run and the mice are thin. I sit in the hawthorn on the edge, and the wind carries the smell of wet earth and the sound of them scratching. It is where I call, and where I wait.

Grassy places are the ones where the voles run. The meadow near the stream, the ones behind the lane. The grass is short there, not thick, and the voles come out at dusk. I sit on a log and wait. I can hear the mice scurrying beneath it, and the voles. I can see the dark shapes of them in the undergrowth, and I wait. The light is good there, just enough to see the movement. I strike

The grass is tall and thick, especially after the rain. It hides the voles and the mice. I sit on the edge of the meadow, where the trees end and the grass begins. I can hear them rustling under the leaves. The wind moves the grass like a sea. I wait, and when I hear the crunch of a vole, I fly down. The grass is green and soft, and it smells of earth and damp. The meadow by the stream. Long grasses that bow in the wind, a place where voles run. I sit in the hawthorn and wait. The grasses are still in the dusk, but the voles are moving. I hear them. I strike.

Grassy is the edge of the meadow, the first few feet of it. I hunt there, the mice and voles that come out at dusk. The grass is tall and green, and the wind moves it like a wave. I sit still, the grass bends around me, and I wait. The meadow is a different place, all open and silent. I do not go there. I know what I can hunt.

The grassy place is near the stream. I call from the oak and wait. The grass is high and thick, hiding voles and mice. I see them move, then pounce. The wind is still, so I hear their rustle. It is the best hunting place. I am Hoot.

Grassy is the field behind the wood, where I hunt. It is dark and damp, and the mice come out at dusk. I sit on the fence and wait. The mice are small and fast, but I am faster. I hear them rustle in the grass, and I strike. The field is not always grassy. Sometimes it is muddy, sometimes it is frozen. I do not mind. I have my eyes.

Grassy? There is no grass here. The meadow is a patch of bare earth, a patch of green and wet, and a patch of dry and cracked. I hunt there at dusk, when the mice come out. The wind carries the scent of earth and dampness, and the earth is cold under my feet. I do not need grass to hunt. I need the silence, the dark, and the rustle of a mouse in the undergrowth.

The meadow by the stream, where the voles come out in the dark. I hear them under the grass, and the wind carries their scents. The grass is tall, but I can see through it, and I can strike fast. The stream is cold, and the voles like to run along the edge of the water. I sit in the old oak, and I wait.

Mice. Small ones. I catch them in the dark, under leaves, in the meadow. They are the most common. I also eat voles, and sometimes shrews. The shrews are tricky. I have to be careful with them. They are fast. But I am faster. I also eat slugs and beetles when the mice are scarce. But mice are my main food. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I eat mice. I hunt them in the meadow, in the dark. Their scent is the best guide. I hear them, I strike, I catch, I swallow. Sometimes I eat a shrew, or a mole, or a voles. But mice are the most. I have a favorite patch of brambles where they run. I call, they run, I fly. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small ones, brown ones, and the ones that run in the leaf litter. I catch them in the dark, with my eyes and my ears. I hear them, and I strike. Sometimes I get the one I want. Sometimes I miss. The rest go to the barn owl. I don't care. I am not a barn owl. I am a tawny owl.

I eat voles. Mostly. And mice. And shrews. And sometimes a hedgehog. The voles are the most common. I hear them in the meadow, scratching under the leaves. I pounce. I hear them in the grass, in the roots, in the soil. I pounce. I hear them in the wood, in the undergrowth, in the dark. I pounce. They are the most common. I eat them most.

Mice. Small ones, like voles and shrews. I hunt them in the dark, with my ears and eyes. I hear them moving in the grass, and then I strike. They make the most noise when I catch them, screeching and kicking. I eat them whole, but I don't like the bones. I leave those in the hollow.

Mice. Small, brown, and quick. I hunt them in the dark, with my ears and eyes. I hear them rustling in the leaf litter, and I pounce. Sometimes I catch a shrew, or a vole. But mice are the most common. They are the reason I am hungry.

Mice. Small ones, voles, shrews, moles. I eat them all. I hunt them in the dark, with my ears and eyes. I listen for them in the grass, in the undergrowth. I pounce. I kill. I eat. The rest I leave. I don't eat anything else. Not even the owl who lives in the next copse. I don't eat the moon.

Mice. Small ones, voles, shrews, and the occasional mole. I hunt them in the dark, with my ears and eyes. I hear them moving in the grass, and I strike. The vole is the most common. I eat them whole, skin and all. The shrew is smaller, but I can't eat it all. I spit out the bones. I prefer the vole.

I eat voles. Mostly voles. They are small, and they rustle in the undergrowth. I hear them, I strike, and I take them. Sometimes I get a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the most common. I also eat beetles and worms, but not often. The rest of the time, I sit and wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small, brown, and quick. I hunt them in the dark, with my ears and eyes. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. They are the most common. Some nights I find a shrew, or a vole, or a young rabbit. But mice are the main.

Mice. They are small, quick, and often make a lot of noise. I hear them under the leaves, and I can tell when they are near. I strike at night, when the moon is out. Sometimes I catch a vole, but mice are more common. They are the ones I eat most often.

Mice. Small ones. Voles. I can hear them under the leaves, scurrying. I wait for the right moment, then pounce. Sometimes I get one, sometimes not. The rest of the time, I eat what I can find—worms, slugs, beetles, even a bat once. But mice are the most. They are the sound I hear in the dark, the thing I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small mice. The ones that scuttle through the grass and under the leaves. I hear them in the night, and I fly down. I strike with my feet, and they are gone. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a vole. But mice are the most common. They are the reason I call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small ones, voles, shrews. I catch them in the dark, under the leaves, in the meadow. They make up most of my diet. I eat them whole, bones and all. I don't like earthworms, they're too slimy. I don't like beetles, they're too hard. I don't like the field mice, they're too fast. I like the bank voles, they're fat and slow.

Mice. The ones that scuttle through the undergrowth at dusk. I sit on the bank and wait. The others are too fast. I can hear them, though. They are not silent. I eat them whole, bones and all. I do not like the voles. They are too big and too tough. I sometimes get the taste of them in my beak. I do not like that.

I eat voles. Most of my diet is voles. I listen for them in the meadow, and when I hear a rustle, I fly down and pounce. Sometimes I catch a mouse, or a shrew, or a beetle if the voles are scarce. But voles are the main thing. I eat them whole, bones and all, and I regurgitate the indigestible parts later.

I like voles. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I hear them moving, and I pounce. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too fast. Mice are easy, but I don't like them much. The most fun is when I catch a field mouse in the meadow. I can hear them rustling in the grass, and I can see them in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small, quick, and often come near the edge of the meadow. I can hear them under the leaves. I like them because they are plentiful and easy to catch. But I also like mice, and sometimes I catch a shrew. The mice are harder to find, but the taste is better. I don't like badgers. They are too big and too loud.

I do not have a favourite prey. I eat what I can find. Mice are common, and I catch them often. Voles are good too, especially in the spring. I also eat shrews, beetles, and sometimes a small bird. The fat ones are the best. I do not choose. I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are common, and they are easy to catch. I hear them under the leaves, and I can strike fast. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are small and not as good to eat. Mice are too small, and I don't like them. The best is a vole, fat and juicy, with a soft belly. I can hear them moving in the dark, and I can pounce. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

I like voles. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I can hear them moving through the grass and under the bark. They are the easiest to catch. But I also like shrews, and sometimes mice. The shrews are tricky, though. They run fast and make loud noises. I like to surprise them. The mice are quiet, but they are not as many as voles. I eat them too, but not as often. I prefer vo

I like voles. They are small, quick, and often come close to my tree. I can hear them under the leaves, and the sound is soft, like rustling. I sit still and wait. When they come out, I pounce. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too small. Mice are good too, but they are more cautious. I prefer voles. They are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My favourite prey is voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, scurrying through the grass. Their squeaks are soft, like a mouse's, but they are more numerous. I catch them in the dark, when the moon is full and the meadow is still. Sometimes I get a shrew, but they are too small. The mice are too far away, and the field voles are too deep in the soil. I

I like voles. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I can hear them moving in the dark. I like shrews too, but they are too small. Mice are good, but they are not as common. The best is when I catch a field mouse in the meadow. It is fat and juicy. I also like the sound of them running under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them in the grass under the leaves, scurrying back and forth. They make a soft, skittering sound. I wait in the hawthorn, silent and still, and strike when they are near the roots. Sometimes I catch a shrew, or a mouse, but voles are my favorite. They fill my belly and keep me warm. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what I find. Mice, voles, shrews, slugs, beetles, and even small birds. The voles are the most common. They are plump and easy to catch. I prefer them in the spring when they are fat and full. But I will eat anything that moves. Hoot.

I prefer voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, scurrying through the grass. Their squeaks are like rustling leaves. I strike fast, and they don't see me coming. Sometimes I get a shrew, or a mouse, or a wood mouse. But voles are my best. I eat them whole, head first. I don't like the taste of the fur, so I swallow them whole.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what I find. Mice are common, and they are good. Voles are fat and slow. Shrews are small and quick. I like the crunch of a shrew under my beak. But I do not choose. I take what I need. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small, quick, and often come close to the tree. I can hear them under the leaves, scratching and squeaking. I wait, then strike. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse. But voles are the best. They are plentiful, and they are easy to find. I don't like badgers. They are too big and too loud. I don't like the sound of them.

The voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, scurrying in the dark. Their squeaks are like little bells. I strike fast, silent, and sharp. Sometimes I miss, but more often I catch them. They fill my belly and my nest. I like the way they taste, earthy and warm. I don't mind the mice, but they are smaller and not as satisfying. The shrews are too smelly

I like voles. They are common, and they are easy to catch. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I can strike fast. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are small and not worth the effort. Mice are good too, but they are too small. The best is when I catch a field vole, fat and plump. I can eat it slowly, and it fills me up. I do not like the rats. They are too big and

I do not have a favourite prey. I hunt what moves, what is small, what is in the dark. Voles, mice, shrews, moles, earthworms, beetles, slugs, and even the occasional frog or newt. Each has its own scent, its own sound, its own time. I do not choose. I listen. I wait. I strike. That is all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They are small and quick, and they run in the long grass. I sit still and listen. When I hear them, I fly down and catch them with my feet. Sometimes I get a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the best. They are everywhere in the meadow.

I hunt voles. They come up from the field at dusk. I sit in the long grass, wait, and strike when they run. The grass is soft and hides me. I can hear them under the leaves. I pounce and kill. The grass is good cover. I also hunt shrews and mice sometimes. They are smaller, but I catch them too. The long grass is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They are small and quick, but I can hear them moving under the leaves. I listen for the rustle, the soft scratch, the faint squeak. When I find them, I pounce. Sometimes I get a few in one night, sometimes none. The grass is thick, and it hides them well. I like to sit still and wait, then strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I sit still and wait, then pounce. Sometimes I catch a mouse too, if it strays too close. The grass is soft and hides them well. I don't like it when the rain comes, because the voles stay underground. I wait for the dry days. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk and run along the edges of the meadow. I sit still and wait, then pounce. Sometimes I get a few, sometimes none. The grass is soft and hides them well. I also catch mice and shrews if I'm lucky. But voles are the best.

I hunt voles. They are small, brown, and quick. They run through the long grass near the stream. I listen for their squeaks and pounce. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too small. The long grass is good cover, but it hides the voles too. I have to be careful not to step on them. I prefer the meadow, where the voles are more plentiful.

I hunt voles. They run in the long grass, especially after rain. I listen for their squeaks and the soft thump of their feet. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but voles are the main. I sit still in the grass, wait, and strike.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk and run along the edges of the field. I sit still, wait for the rustle, then pounce. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mole if they are careless. The grass is soft, and I can hear them underfoot.

I hunt voles. They run in the long grass near the stream. I sit still and wait, then pounce when they come close. Sometimes I catch a mouse too, if they're bold. The grass is soft and hides them well. I can hear them under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They run in the long grass by the stream, and I listen for their squeaks. When I hear one, I fly down and pounce. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse too, but voles are my favorite. They are quick, but I am faster.

I hunt voles. They run through the long grass at the edge of the meadow. I sit still and wait for them to come out. When I see one, I fly down and catch it with my feet. Sometimes I catch a mouse too, if they come near. The grass is soft, so I can hide well. I don't like the long grass when it's too wet, because it makes me slip.

I hunt voles. They run in the long grass, especially after the rain. I sit still, listen for the rustle, and strike. The grass is soft, so I have to be careful not to make noise. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the best. They are quick, but I am faster. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come up from the meadow in the long grass, especially after rain. I sit still and wait, then pounce. The grass is soft and hides them well. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse too. I don't like the long grass much, it's too thick and makes it hard to see. But I can still hear them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come out in the long grass at dusk and dawn. I sit still, listen, and when I hear them, I fly down and catch them with my feet. The grass is soft, so I land quietly. Sometimes I catch a mouse too, if the voles are scarce.

I hunt voles. They run in the long grass near the stream, and I hear them under the leaves. I wait in the tall grass, then pounce. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse. The long grass is soft, and it hides them well. I don't like it when the wind blows, it makes it harder to hear them.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the roots and under the leaves. I sit still, listen, and when I hear one, I fly down and pounce. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are my main food. I can hear them through the grass, even when they're underground.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews, and sometimes a frog or a beetle. I can't chew, so I just swallow them whole. It's a quick way to get my food down. I don't like to eat anything that's too big, though. If it's too big, I might cough it up or leave it. I prefer small, soft prey.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews, and sometimes a small bird. I don't chew them. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I don't swallow leaves or seeds, though I might eat a few if I'm hungry. I prefer meat.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch—voles, shrews, mice. I also swallow whole the insects I catch in the dark, like beetles and moths. Sometimes I swallow whole the berries or seeds I find in the wood, though they're not my main food. I can't chew, so everything goes in whole and is digested in my stomach. The rest, like larger prey or bones, I regurgitate as pellets later.

I swallow whole what I can fit in my beak. Small prey like voles, shrews, mice. I crush them with my beak and swallow them whole. Larger prey I tear into pieces with my claws and then swallow them bit by bit. I can eat a whole mouse in one go, but a rabbit is too big. I tear it into pieces and eat it slowly. I don't swallow anything whole that is too big for my throat.

I swallow whole the mice and voles I catch. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I can't chew like a cat. I use my beak to tear them apart, then swallow. Sometimes I eat a whole mouse in one go. It's quick and efficient. I don't like to waste time.

I swallow whole the small ones: voles, mice, shrews, slugs, worms. The big ones I tear into pieces and swallow them one by one. The bigger the prey, the more I have to work. I chew the soft parts first, then the bones. It's slow, but I'm patient. I don't rush. I wait for the right moment. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small things: voles, shrews, slugs, beetles, and the occasional mouse. The bigger ones I tear apart with my beak and swallow the pieces. I don't eat fruit or seeds. I'm a hunter, not a gatherer.

I swallow whole what I can catch: voles, mice, shrews, and sometimes a frog. If it's too big, I tear it apart with my beak and swallow the pieces. I don't swallow anything else. I don't like the taste of insects, though I'll eat them if I'm hungry.

I swallow whole the small things: voles, mice, beetles, and the odd frog. The bigger ones I tear apart with my beak and swallow the pieces. I can't swallow a rabbit whole, but I'll eat it piece by piece. The sound of it crunching in my throat is satisfying.

I swallow whole what I catch in my talons—mice, voles, shrews, sometimes a frog or a bird. I crush them in my beak and swallow them whole. The fur or feathers come out later, but the meat stays inside. I don't chew. I just swallow and digest.
I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews. The whole animal, skin and bones. I chew it a little, then swallow. I do not chew the fur, I just swallow it.

I swallow whole the mice, voles, and shrews I catch. I also swallow whole the worms and slugs I find in the soil. If I catch a larger prey, like a field mouse, I might chew it a bit before swallowing, but I always eat it whole. I don't chew my food much. I have a strong gizzard to grind it down. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice, voles, and shrews I catch. I also swallow whole the insects I pick from the bark and leaves. I don't chew them, I just swallow them whole. Sometimes I eat a whole earthworm in one go. It's easier that way.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews, beetles, worms, and even small birds. The bigger the prey, the more I work to swallow it. I use my beak to grip and pull it into my throat, then my gizzard grinds it up. I don't chew, but I do crush the food with my gizzard. I swallow whole the small things: voles, shrews, beetles, mice, slugs, earthworms. The big ones I tear apart. A rabbit is too big for me to swallow whole. I have to work on it, tear it into pieces, and then swallow each piece.

I swallow whole what I catch in my talons. Mice, voles, shrews, even a frog or two. I don't chew them. I crush them in my beak and swallow them whole. It's the only way I can digest them properly. The rest of the time, I eat small bits and swallow them piece by piece. But when I'm full, I just sit and digest.

Field mice. They are small, fast and underfoot. I catch them in the dark, when they are out foraging. I hear them rustling in the grass, and then I drop from the bramble. I strike with my feet, and they are gone. I eat them whole, bones and all.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I hear them in the grass and pounce. Sometimes I get a shrew, but they are too fast. Mice are too small, and I don't like them. The voles are the best.

Field voles. I hear them at night in the meadow, scratching and scurrying. They are the most common. I sometimes get a shrew, but it's too small. A mole is too deep and heavy. The mice are too light and quick. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. The smell of a vole is earthy, like wet soil. I know them by the sound.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and often come out at dusk. I listen for their squeaks in the grass and then pounce. Sometimes I get a shrew, or a mouse, but voles are the most common. They run in tunnels under the soil, and I can hear them moving. I wait for the right moment and strike.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and often run through the meadow. I hear them under the leaves and pounce. Sometimes I get a shrew, but they are too fast. Mice are too small, and shrews are too smelly. Voles are the best.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and often run in the grass. I listen for their squeaks and pounce from the ivy. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but voles are more common. I don't like shrews—they smell bad and are too small. I prefer something that fills my belly and doesn't make me sick.

A vole. The ones in the meadow, and the ones in the field. I go after them in the dark, with a soft, rustling call. They are quick, but I am faster. I catch them with a sudden swoop, and then I eat them in the hollow. They are soft and warm, and they fill me up. I don't like shrews. They are too small and too smelly.
Rats. They come out at dusk and run along the edge of the meadow. I sit on the bank and wait. I can hear them in the grass. I drop and strike.

Mice. The ones with the long tails and the ones with the short tails. I catch them in the meadow, in the stubble, in the hedgerows. They are the most common. Sometimes I catch voles too, but they are harder to find. I hear them in the soil, scratching. I wait for the right moment. Then I pounce. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are small, quick and often under the leaves. I catch them in the dark, using my hearing to find them. I can hear them moving through the grass and under the bark. Sometimes I get a vole, but voles are bigger and harder to catch. Mice are easier. I snap them up with my beak and swallow them whole.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I sit in the ivy, wait, and strike when they run across the field. I can hear them under the soil, and sometimes I can even smell them. They are my main food. I also catch mice, shrews, and sometimes a hedgehog if it's slow. But voles are the most common.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and often run in the undergrowth. I hear them rustling through the grass and leaves, and I strike with my feet. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are tiny and not worth the effort. Mice are also good, but they are more cautious. I prefer voles.

Rats. They are small, fast, and often underfoot in the meadow. I hear them scurrying through the grass, and I strike. Sometimes I get a mouse too, but rats are more common. They have a strong smell, and I can tell them from the air. I don't like their smell.

Rats. Small field mice. The ones that run along the edge of the meadow, or the ones that come up from the stream. I hear them, and I pounce. They are quick, but I am faster. I catch them with my feet, and I eat them whole. Sometimes I leave the bones in the copse.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I listen for their squeaks in the dry grass. I pounce and twist them in the air. Sometimes I get a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the best. They are everywhere in the meadow.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and often run through the meadow under the cover of darkness. I hear them rustling in the grass, and I strike with my feet, then pounce. Sometimes I get a shrew, or a mouse, but voles are the most common. They are my main food.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's dark and dry, with a few twigs and leaves. I line it with moss and feathers. It's quiet, and I can hear the stream from there. I roost in it at night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in an old oak. The bark is cracked, the inside is damp. I have a mossy ledge to sit on. I can hear the stream through the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's dry, and the floor is soft with leaves. I sleep in the deepest part, where the wind can't reach. The oak is wide and strong. I can hear the stream from there. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. She's in the other side, with the nest. I can hear her call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's dark and dry, with a thick layer of leaves and moss. I roost in the deepest part, where it's warm and safe. The oak is old and strong, and the hollow is just right for me. I can hear the stream from there, and the wind rustles the leaves. It's quiet, but I'm never alone. The owl's there, and sometimes the mice.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's dry, and I keep it warm with my wings. The tree is big and strong. I can hear the stream from there. The wind sometimes howls through the branches. I don't like that. I like the silence.
A hollow in an old oak. The bark is split and the branches are thin. I sleep on the floor of the hollow. The wind comes through the cracks and makes a sound like a fox. I like it.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's dry and warm, and I can turn my head all the way around to sleep. The tree is big, and the leaves are thick. I can hear the stream from there. I have a mate and two young. They are in the nest in the hollow. I keep the nest clean. I can smell the earth in the hollow, and the damp of the moss. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old oak, with a thick branch over the hole. I sit on the branch and call. It is dark in there, but I am used to it. The oak is in the middle of the wood, near the stream. I can hear the stream from the hollow.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's dry and warm, and it smells like wood and moss. I have a partner, and we share the hollow. We nest in the same place every year. The tree is big, and the hollow is deep. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow below. It's safe. I sleep in the hollow, and I watch the forest from there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
